comments.author: @imacuser101
comments.text: It was good reporting until you said you wanted to wait and see for the water use on the data center. Those closed loop systems are deployed in many locations, and they will only be closed loop. So, in aggregate to fill, it'll be very expensive. But day to day, you're looping water and pipes. The only thing you have to account for is leakage. There's nothing crazy about it.

replies.author: @FrankRamirezVF
replies.text: That’s a fair distinction: closed-loop systems change the day-to-day picture a lot, because the steady-state water demand is much lower than once-through cooling. The remaining question is the aggregate buildout around a campus this large, since even “normal” operation can still mean material fill, maintenance, and contingency planning when you scale it across many buildings. - Francisco Ramirez, LinkedIn

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: Yes, closed-loop cooling is established technology, but the water demand also depends on how the heat leaves that loop. If it uses evaporative cooling towers, those still need replacement water; if it uses dry cooling, that’s a different picture. My caution was about the broader water footprint, rather than whether recirculating water works.

comments.author: @HiddenEnginesExplained
comments.text: The discussion of power delivery at 9:04 points to an important distinction: generating electricity and getting it to a particular site are separate engineering tasks. Transmission lines, substations and connections all need to accommodate the load. More generation alone does not remove every local bottleneck. I explain how that delivery chain works, from power plants to the final circuit, in a video on my channel.

replies.author: @FrankRamirezVF
replies.text: Exactly, and that distinction is easy to miss in these mega-project stories. Even if generation is available, the site still depends on transmission, substation capacity, and the last-mile interconnect, which is where local bottlenecks often show up. That’s why the corridor around Savannah matters as much as the headline load number. - Francisco Ramirez, LinkedIn

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: Exactly. A region can have enough generation overall and still struggle to deliver power to one particular site. That’s what makes the substation and transmission capacity so important to where these campuses land. I did a deeper dive on that issue, in particular, in Virginia: https://youtu.be/4zNCZylGwfE
